n_randomized: 32 neonates randomised to three formula groups (A, B, C); 10 additional infants fed human milk (not randomised)
population: Very-low-birth-weight neonates, birth weight 1000-1500 g; GA not reported in abstract
intervention_dose_duration: Formula diets of differing omega-3 content from day 10 to day 45 or discharge, whichever occurred first: Group A predominantly 18:2 omega-6; Group B balanced 18:2 omega-6 and 18:3 omega-3; Group C essential fatty acids plus marine oil supplementation to provide 22:6 omega-3 similar to human milk. Doses not reported in abstract
primary_outcome: Retinal function by electroretinogram (cone function; rod ERG thresholds). Primary outcome not explicitly stated in abstract
key_findings: Plasma and RBC fatty acid profiles similar at entry, diverged after diets. Group C comparable to human milk-fed group; Group A had lower 22:6 omega-3 and omega-3 LCPUFA. Cone function unaffected by dietary EFA. Group A rod ERG thresholds higher than human milk and Group C; correlated with RBC omega-3 LCPUFA (r = -0.63, p<0.0001); 44% of variance explained by RBC and plasma omega-3 LCPUFA.

n_randomized: Not stated in the abstract provided
population: Healthy preterm infants; gestational age and birth weight inclusion criteria not stated in the abstract provided
intervention_dose_duration: Formula with marine oil as a source of DHA versus standard formula without marine oil; dose/concentration, start, and duration not stated in the abstract provided. Visual acuity followed to approximately 6.5 months of age
primary_outcome: Visual acuity measured by the Teller Acuity Card procedure
key_findings: Marine oil (P < 0.001) and age (P < 0.0001) influenced visual acuity (repeated-measures ANOVA). Marine-oil group had better acuity than standard-formula group at 2 and 4 months (Fisher's LSD). Acuity improved in both groups through 6.5 months, then plateaued. Through 4 months, acuity was inversely related to oxygen supplementation (log10 h) and positively related to DHA status (GLM). After 4 months, birth weight and gestational age were the only consistent correlates.

n_randomized: 59 preterm infants (randomized; double-blind trial)
population: Preterm infants, birth weight 747-1275 g; some required prolonged supplemental oxygen and developed bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Gestational age inclusion not stated in abstract.
intervention_dose_duration: Formula containing long-chain n-3 fatty acids (n-3 LCFAs) from marine oil vs control formula containing linolenic acid (LLA) as sole n-3 fatty acid; dose, start and duration not stated in abstract. Infants studied at 0, 2, 4, 6, 9, and 12 months past term.
primary_outcome: Visual acuity (Teller Acuity Card) and growth (weight, length, head circumference, weight-for-length); plasma phosphatidylcholine arachidonic acid. Primary outcome not explicitly designated in abstract.
key_findings: n-3 LCFAs improved early (2-mo) but not later acuity among infants without BPD (P<0.02). Infants with BPD had poorer grating acuity at 2 (P<0.0002) and 4 (P<0.04) mo regardless of diet. n-3 LCFA infants weighed less at 6 and 9 mo and had smaller head circumference at 9 mo; lower weight-for-length at 2, 6, 9, 12 mo. Plasma PC AA not influenced by BPD or n-3 LCFAs.

n_randomized: 19 randomized to formula groups (10 without LCP, 9 with LCP); 8 additional infants received their own mother's milk fortified with FM-85 (not randomized); 27 enrolled in total
population: Low birthweight infants enrolled when tolerating full enteral feeding (≥130 ml milk/kg/day). Mean birthweight ~1218–1280 g and mean gestational age ~30–31 weeks across groups (mean ± SD as reported)
intervention_dose_duration: LBWI formula (Prematil, Milupa AG) with LCP providing docosahexaenoic and arachidonic acids at levels similar to average human milk, versus the same formula without LCP, given in blinded batches; comparator group received mother's milk fortified with FM-85 (5 g/100 ml milk); study period 21 days
primary_outcome: Not stated in the provided abstract (truncated); growth and feeding tolerance (gastric residuals, spitting, abdominal distention, stool firmness) are reported outcomes
key_findings: Three feeding groups did not differ in growth or feeding tolerance (gastric residuals, spitting, abdominal distention) over 21 days; firm stools were noted more frequently in the two formula groups. Abstract truncated at 250 words, so further findings are not available.

n_randomized: 58 healthy preterm infants enrolled (breast milk n=12; PF-LCP n=21; PF n=25); note the abstract describes the groups as fed by feeding type and does not explicitly state randomisation
population: Healthy preterm infants; gestational age and birth weight inclusion criteria not stated in the abstract
intervention_dose_duration: Feeding groups: breast milk (n=12); preterm formula supplemented with long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (PF-LCP, n=21); traditional preterm formula (PF, n=25). LCP dose, DHA concentration, start age and feeding duration not stated in the abstract; outcomes assessed at 52 weeks postconceptional age
primary_outcome: Not explicitly designated in the abstract. Outcomes assessed: flash visual evoked potentials (VEPs), flash electroretinography (ERG), brainstem acoustic evoked potentials (BAEPs), and red blood cell membrane fatty acid composition
key_findings: Breast milk and PF-LCP groups had similar VEP morphology and latencies; PF group had quite different morphology and significantly longer wave latencies. Erythrocyte LCP, especially DHA, was higher in breast milk and PF-LCP groups than PF. ERG and BAEP were the same in all three groups. Authors suggest well-balanced LCP supplementation may positively influence VEP maturation when breast milk is unavailable.

n_randomized: 30 infants randomised into three arms of 10 each (LCP-enriched preterm formula, standard preterm formula, or expressed breast milk); double-blind, prospective
population: Healthy preterm infants during the first weeks of life; gestational age and birth weight inclusion criteria not stated in abstract
intervention_dose_duration: LCP-enriched preterm formula vs standard preterm formula vs (expressed) breast milk; study period 3 weeks; LCP dose not stated in abstract
primary_outcome: In vivo formation of prostaglandin E2, thromboxane A2 and prostacyclin, measured as urinary excretion of index metabolites by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry; urine sampled and anthropometric measurements at study entry and after 3 weeks
key_findings: No significant differences in urinary prostanoid excretion or anthropometric data between groups at end of study. Conclusion: neither conventional formula nor LCP supplementation for 3 weeks substantially influenced prostanoid formation in healthy preterm infants.

n_randomized: Not stated in abstract (randomized, double-masked clinical study of diet and infant neurodevelopment; hospitalized preterm infants)
population: Hospitalized preterm infants; gestational age and birth weight inclusion criteria not stated in abstract
intervention_dose_duration: Experimental preterm formula containing egg phospholipids (provided 7-fold more esterified choline, arachidonic acid 0.4% of total fatty acids, docosahexaenoic acid 0.13%) versus commercial control preterm formula; start and duration not stated in abstract
primary_outcome: Not explicitly stated in abstract; reported outcome was incidence of stage II and III necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC)
key_findings: Stage II and III NEC was significantly lower with the experimental formula than control (2.9% vs 17.6%, p < 0.05). Rates of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (23.4% vs 23.5%), septicemia (26% vs 31%), and retinopathy of prematurity (38% vs 40%) were similar. Authors state a larger randomized trial is warranted.

n_randomized: 288 enrolled; 77 supplemented formula, 78 control formula, 133 human milk (human milk group not randomised; formula groups randomised)
population: Preterm infants; GA/BW inclusion criteria not stated in the abstract
intervention_dose_duration: LCPUFA-supplemented preterm formula (long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids from single-cell algal and fungal oils) vs unsupplemented control preterm formula vs human milk; dose, start, and duration not stated in the abstract; follow-up to 48 weeks postconceptional age
primary_outcome: Not specified in the abstract. Outcomes reported: growth (anthropometrics at enrollment, first day of full oral feeding, 40 and 48 weeks PCA), acceptance (discontinuation, reasons, adverse events), and plasma fatty acid concentrations
key_findings: Growth at enrollment, first full oral feeding, 40 and 48 weeks PCA did not differ between formula groups; human milk group initially grew more slowly. Severe adverse events were rare and not significantly different between formula groups. Supplemented formula and human milk groups had higher LCPUFA concentrations than control formula. Authors conclude safety and efficacy of the supplemented formula.

n_randomized: Breast milk group n = 15 (4 dropped out); formula A (18-carbon PUFA only) n = 11 (2 dropped out); formula B (enriched with long-chain PUFA) n = 14 (1 dropped out). Note: the BM group was fed breast milk and not randomised; only A and B were randomly assigned.
population: Preterm infants enrolled on the 2nd day of enteral feeding (D0); gestational age and birth weight inclusion criteria not reported in the abstract.
intervention_dose_duration: Breast milk (BM) or random assignment to formula A (containing only 18-carbon PUFA) or formula B (enriched with long-chain PUFA), fed for at least 30 days (to D30). Doses not reported in the abstract.
primary_outcome: Early neurological maturation: auditory and visual evoked potential parameters and nerve conduction velocity (NCV), with plasma and red blood cell phospholipid fatty acid composition, measured at D0 and D30. (Abstract does not explicitly designate a primary outcome.)
key_findings: No difference between groups in D0-D30 changes in EP parameters. Motor NCV maturation slower in group B than the other two groups. Plasma linoleic acid changes higher in B than BM and A (P<0.05); arachidonic acid changes higher in BM vs B (P<0.02). RBC linoleic acid higher in formula groups than BM (P<0.05). No group differences in arachidonic or docosahexaenoic acid changes. Authors conclude a balanced n-6/n-3 PUFA supply without LC-PUFA allowed adequate early CNS maturation; LC-PUFA effects on NCV need confirmation.

n_randomized: 63 infants (32 males; 31 females) randomised; blinded RCT, May 1993 to September 1994
population: Healthy low-birth-weight preterm infants, birth weight 940-2250 g; enrolled around hospital discharge (feeding began 7-10 days before discharge)
intervention_dose_duration: Preterm formula with or without DHA (22:6n3, 0.2 wt%, from fish oil) from 7-10 days before discharge to 43 weeks PMA; then term formula with or without a corresponding amount of DHA from 43 to 59 weeks PMA. Control: formula without DHA.
primary_outcome: Not stated in the abstract. Outcomes evaluated: weight, length, head circumference; skinfold thicknesses (triceps, subscapular, suprailiac); arm, abdominal and chest circumferences; fat-free mass (FFM) by total body electrical conductivity (TOBEC); energy intake from formula.
key_findings: In males, DHA formula gave smaller gains in weight, length and head circumference to 59 weeks PMA (P<0.05); at 59 weeks lower weight (P<0.05), shorter recumbent length (P<0.01), smaller head circumference (P<0.05) and lower FFM (P<0.01). No significant differences in females. Male energy intake lower at 51 and 59 weeks (P<0.05) but not significant when adjusted for body weight. Authors conclude DHA formula had a negative effect on male growth and body composition; they do not support adding DHA alone to formulas.

n_randomized: 17 infants fed LCP-F (formula with n-6 and n-3 LCP from purified pig-brain phospholipids); 17 infants fed conventional formula F; 14 infants receiving human milk from a milk bank as reference (HM). Note: the abstract describes groups as "were fed" and does not explicitly state randomisation.
population: Low birth-weight infants; gestational age and birth-weight inclusion criteria not stated in the abstract
intervention_dose_duration: LCP-F: formula with n-6 and n-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids from purified pig-brain phospholipids; comparator F: conventional low-birth-weight formula; HM: human milk from a milk bank (reference). Feeding duration 30 days; blood sampled at entry, day 15 and day 30. Dose/concentration not stated in the abstract.
primary_outcome: Not explicitly stated in the abstract. Stated aims: plasma content of 20:4n-6 and 22:6n-3 and plasma antioxidant capacity. Growth index was also measured.
key_findings: Plasma 22:6n-3 was higher in LCP-F than F and closer to HM throughout. Total plasma lipid DHA at 15 days: 3.46±0.19 vs 2.08±0.20 mg/dl (P<0.001); at 30 days: 3.83±0.30 vs 2.15±0.20 mg/dl (P<0.001). 20:4n-6 was higher in LCP-F than F at 15 and 30 days. Plasma antioxidant capacity did not differ significantly between groups.

n_randomized: 66 premature infants randomized (human milk group was nonrandomized)
population: Premature infants; gestational age and birth weight inclusion criteria not stated in the abstract
intervention_dose_duration: Four randomized formulas: ST (no GLA, no LCPUFA); BO (0.6% GLA from borage oil); BO + FOLOW (0.6% GLA, 0.3% DHA, 0.06% EPA); BO + FOHIGH (0.6% GLA, 0.3% DHA, 0.2% EPA). Nonrandomized human milk (HM) comparison group. Duration 4 weeks; measurements at study entry, day 14 and day 28.
primary_outcome: Not stated in the abstract. Outcomes reported: anthropometric measures, tocopherol and retinol status, and arachidonic acid (AA) content of plasma phospholipids.
key_findings: No significant between-group differences in anthropometrics, tocopherol or retinol status. Plasma phospholipid AA was similar at study start and decreased by day 28 in all formula groups but not in breast-fed infants (ST 6.6 +/- 0.2%, BO 6.9 +/- 0.3%, BO + FOLOW 6.9 +/- 0.4%, BO + FOHIGH 6.7 +/- 0.2%, HM 8.6 +/- 0.5%; all formulas P<0.05 vs HM). GLA or fish oil addition had no significant influence; GLA had only a very limited effect on AA status.

n_randomized: 470 formula-fed (3 arms) + 43 human-milk reference
intervention_dose_duration: AA+DHA from fish/fungal or egg-TG/fish oils, to 12 mo CA
primary_outcome: Growth, visual acuity, development
key_findings: Growth not impaired; some developmental and visual measures favoured LCPUFA arms at 6–14 mo CA (abstract-level).

n_randomized: 194 premature infants (randomized to control, DHA, or DHA+ARA preterm formula; 90 breast-fed term infants served as reference, not randomized)
population: Formula-fed premature infants; gestational age/birth weight inclusion criteria not stated in the abstract
intervention_dose_duration: Preterm formula with no DHA/ARA (control), 0.15% energy DHA, or 0.14% DHA + 0.27% ARA from single-cell triglycerides, for at least 28 days; then term formula (no DHA or ARA) to 57 weeks postmenstrual age
primary_outcome: Not stated in the abstract (growth and visual acuity were the study aims; growth outcomes reported as weight gain, weight, weight:length ratio, and length; visual acuity and adverse events also reported)
key_findings: DHA+ARA infants gained weight faster during preterm feeding than control (34.7 vs. 30.7 g/d; post-hoc analysis). DHA+ARA weights and weight:length ratios did not differ from term breast-fed infants at 48 and 57 weeks PMA; control and DHA groups were lighter than term infants. RBC PE ARA correlated with weight gain and with weight and length at 40, 48, and 57 weeks PMA (r = 0.19 to 0.24). DHA or DHA+ARA had no effect on visual acuity or adverse event incidence.

n_randomized: 195 formula-fed preterm infants randomised (plus 88 breast milk-fed infants, not randomised)
population: Preterm infants with birth weight <1750 g and gestation <37 weeks, from 2 UK neonatal units; formula-fed infants randomised, breast milk-fed infants included as a non-randomised comparison group
intervention_dose_duration: Preterm formula with vs. without preformed LCPUFA (double-blind); dose, preparation, start and duration not specified in the abstract. Intervention period during the first weeks of life.
primary_outcome: Bayley Mental Developmental Index (MDI) and Psychomotor Developmental Index (PDI) at 18 months corrected age. Secondary/other: Knobloch, Passamanick and Sherrard Developmental Screening Inventory at 9 months corrected age; anthropometry at 9 and 18 months; tolerance, infection, necrotizing enterocolitis, death.
key_findings: No significant between-group differences in developmental scores. LCPUFA infants showed non-significant 2.6-point (0.25 SD) advantage in MDI and PDI at 18 months; larger non-significant advantage below 30 weeks (MDI 4.5, PDI 5.8). LCPUFA infants shorter at 18 months (length SDS difference 0.44; 95% CI 0.08-0.8). No other significant safety differences. Breastfed infants had higher developmental scores than both formula groups.

n_randomized: 40 infants (20 per group)
population: Preterm infants; gestational age and birth weight inclusion criteria not stated in the abstract. Groups similar at study start for birth weight, gestational age, weight, and corrected age.
intervention_dose_duration: Preterm formula with LCP blend (similar LCP content to human milk) vs. formula without LCP (F); double-blind; 30 days. Mineral balance measured after 1 week.
primary_outcome: Not explicitly stated in the abstract. Outcomes reported: plasma Ca, P, Mg, Zn, Cu (baseline and day 30); nutritional mineral balance (intake, net retention, fecal losses) after 1 week.
key_findings: No differences in mineral balance between F and F+LCP groups for Ca, P, Mg, Zn, or Cu. Plasma mineral concentrations did not change within groups and were comparable between groups; all values were within normal range for age. Milk intake, weight gain, and longitudinal growth were comparable and satisfactory.

n_randomized: 42 formula-fed premature infants
population: Preterm infants; formula-fed; GA/BW inclusion criteria not reported in abstract. Excluded: significant cerebral damage, retinopathy, chronic disease, or feeding problems
intervention_dose_duration: Standard preterm formula (control) vs identical formula supplemented with DHA 0.015 g/100 ml and ARA 0.031 g/100 ml; duration not reported in abstract; prospective, double-blind, randomized
primary_outcome: Not stated as primary; outcomes assessed were cerebral myelination by MRI, psychomotor and mental development, visual development, and flash visual evoked potentials (latencies); visual acuity also reported
key_findings: Supplementation did not positively influence myelination progress, mental/motor development, or VEP latencies. Visual acuity slightly better in supplemented infants at each test age, but not statistically significant. No demonstrable positive effect on structural brain maturation.

n_randomized: 29 infants randomised to formula devoid of LCP or LCP-supplemented formula; plus 17 breast-fed infants as a control group (not randomised)
population: Preterm infants (gestational age and birth weight inclusion criteria not stated in the abstract)
intervention_dose_duration: Formula enriched with n-6 and n-3 LCP (0.5 g/100 g fat linoleic acid metabolites; 0.8 g/100 g fat alpha-linolenic acid metabolites) vs. formula devoid of LCP; four-week study period; double-blind; sampling at study entry, two weeks and four weeks
primary_outcome: Not stated in the abstract (outcomes reported: plasma fatty acid profiles, antioxidant status (plasma alpha-tocopherol, urinary malondialdehyde), growth, and food/milk tolerance)
key_findings: At four weeks, plasma DHA was significantly higher in supplemented vs unsupplemented infants and similar to breast-fed infants. Plasma n-6 LCP including AA were similar between groups. Alpha-tocopherol of breast-fed and supplemented infants was similar and tended lower than the LCP-free formula group. Urinary MDA was higher in formula-fed than breast-fed infants, with no difference between formula groups. Growth and milk tolerance did not differ between groups.

n_randomized: 238 preterm infants randomly assigned (unsupplemented or LCPUFA-supplemented formula)
population: Preterm infants <35 weeks gestational age and ≤2000 g birth weight
intervention_dose_duration: LCPUFA-supplemented formula containing gamma-linolenic acid (GLA, precursor of arachidonic acid) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) vs unsupplemented formula; supplementation from randomisation to 9 months after term (dose not stated in abstract)
primary_outcome: Bayley Mental Developmental Index (MDI) and Psychomotor Development Index (PDI) at 18 months after term
key_findings: No significant overall between-group differences in neurodevelopment. Preplanned subgroup: LCPUFA-supplemented boys had higher Bayley MDI (difference 5.7 points; 95% CI 0.3 to 11.1; P=.04). LCPUFA infants had greater weight gain birth–9 months (310 g; 95% CI 30 to 590; P=.03) and length gain (1.0 cm; 95% CI 0.02 to 1.9; P=.05), greater in boys. No adverse effects reported.

n_randomized: 60 randomised (control n=22; DHA+ARA(FF) n=20; DHA+ARA(EF) n=18)
population: Preterm infants, birth weight 750-1800 g and gestational age <33 wk; enrolled within 72 h of first enteral feeding
intervention_dose_duration: Three formulas: control (no DHA/ARA); DHA+ARA from fish/fungal oil [DHA+ARA(FF)]; or DHA+ARA from egg/fish oil [DHA+ARA(EF)]. Preterm formula with 0.26% DHA and 0.42% ARA to term corrected age, then 0.16% DHA and 0.42% ARA to 12 mo corrected age (post-discharge formula or breast milk). Human milk allowed by maternal choice.
primary_outcome: Growth and body composition (measured by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry) to 12 mo gestation-corrected age. Abstract does not explicitly designate a single primary outcome.
key_findings: No significant group differences at any time point in weight, length, or head circumference; bone mineral content and density did not differ. At 12 mo CA, DHA+ARA groups had significantly greater lean body mass (p<0.05) and less fat mass (p<0.05) than control. DHA+ARA formulas supported normal growth and bone mineralization.

n_randomized: 361 preterm infants randomized across three formula groups (control, algal-DHA, fish-DHA); term breast-fed reference group n = 105
population: Preterm infants (GA and BW inclusion criteria not stated in the abstract); term breast-fed infants (≥4 months) as reference group
intervention_dose_duration: Infant formulas containing DHA and ARA: algal-DHA group (DHA from algal oil, ARA from fungal oil) vs fish-DHA group (DHA from fish oil, ARA from fungal oil) vs control (no supplementation); fed until 92 weeks PMA, with follow-up to 118 weeks PMA (dose/concentration not stated in the abstract)
primary_outcome: Not specified in the abstract. Outcomes reported: growth, tolerance, adverse events, and Bayley development scores
key_findings: Algal-DHA group weight significantly greater than control from 66 to 118 weeks PMA, and fish-DHA group at 118 weeks PMA; neither differed from term infants at 118 weeks PMA. Algal-DHA group longer than control at 48, 79, 92 weeks PMA; fish-DHA longer at 57, 79, 92 weeks PMA. Supplemented groups had higher Bayley mental and psychomotor scores at 118 weeks PMA than control. Supplementation did not increase morbidity or adverse events.

n_randomized: 27 infants randomised (16 supplemented group; 11 non-supplemented group); double-blind, randomised, comparative study
population: Preterm infants with gestational age 30-37 weeks; active intervention entry required body weight over 2000 g, gestational age over 32 weeks, and full feeding status
intervention_dose_duration: Neoangelac Plus formula with DHA and AA supplementation vs. Neoangelac formula without AA and DHA; active intervention period of 6 months. Dose not reported in abstract.
primary_outcome: Not stated as primary outcome in abstract. Outcomes assessed: cognitive development (Mental Development Index, MDI), Physical Development Index (PDI), visual acuity, physical examination variables, vital signs, and adverse events. Timepoints: 6 months and 1 year.
key_findings: MDI at 6 months 96.1 +/- 8.6 (supplemented) vs 91.7 +/- 10.4 (control); at 1 year 98.7 +/- 8.0 vs 90.5 +/- 6.9. PDI at 6 months 102.2 +/- 10.5 vs 95.4 +/- 13.2; at 1 year 98.0 +/- 5.8 vs 86.7 +/- 11.1. Repeated-measures ANOVA significant between-group differences for MDI and PDI (p = 0.020 and 0.008). No differences in visual acuity, physical examination variables or vital signs; no obvious adverse effects.

n_randomized: 60 newborns entered the study; group A (ω-6/ω-3 2/1) n=24 analysed; group B (ω-6/ω-3 1/1) n=21 analysed; control group n=25 (SEN1500 project, exclusively breast-fed)
population: Very preterm newborns <1500 g and/or <32 weeks gestational age
intervention_dose_duration: Randomised to formula milk with ω-6/ω-3 ratio 2/1 (group A) or 1/1 (group B) during the first year of life; arachidonic acid values reported at 12 months; followed up for 2 years
primary_outcome: Psychomotor development assessed with the Brunet Lézine scale at 24 months corrected age (growth, visual-evoked potentials, brainstem auditory-evoked potentials and plasma fatty acids were also measured periodically)
key_findings: At 12 months, AA was higher in group A than B (6.95 ± 1.55% vs 4.55 ± 0.78%) and PUFA higher (41.02 ± 2.09% vs 38.08 ± 2.32%). Brunet Lézine at 24 months was higher in group A than B (99.9 ± 9 vs 90.8 ± 11, p=0.028); group A similar to controls (100.5 ± 7). No significant differences in growth or evoked potentials between formula groups.

n_randomized: 141 infants randomized (double-blind, placebo-controlled)
population: Human milk-fed preterm infants with birth weight <1500 g
intervention_dose_duration: DHA 32 mg and ARA 31 mg per 100 mL human milk; started 1 week after birth and continued until hospital discharge (mean ~9 weeks). Control: placebo.
primary_outcome: Cognitive development at 6 months of age, assessed with the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ) and event-related potentials (ERPs) as a measure of recognition memory
key_findings: No difference in adverse events or growth between groups. At 6 months, intervention group had better problem-solving subscore (53.4 vs 49.5); total score higher but nonsignificant (221 vs 215). ERP: significantly lower responses to standard image (8.6 vs 13.2); no difference for novel images. Authors concluded early DHA/ARA supplementation was associated with better recognition memory and higher problem-solving scores at 6 months.

comparator: standard DHA (~0.3% TFA; soy oil capsules)
n_randomized: 657 infants enrolled (93.5% completed 18-month follow-up)
population: Preterm infants born at less than 33 weeks' gestation; enrolled April 2001 to October 2005 at 5 Australian tertiary hospitals
intervention_dose_duration: High-DHA enteral feeds (approximately 1% total fatty acids) vs standard DHA (approximately 0.3% total fatty acids), from day 2 to 4 of life until term corrected age
primary_outcome: Bayley Mental Development Index (MDI) at 18 months' corrected age
key_findings: No overall MDI difference between high- and standard-DHA groups (mean difference 1.9; 95% CI -1.0 to 4.7). Girls on high DHA had higher MDI (adjusted mean difference 4.5; 95% CI 0.5-8.5); boys showed no difference. Birth weight <1250 g: unadjusted difference 4.7 (95% CI 0.2-9.2), not significant after adjustment (3.8; 95% CI -0.5 to 8.0). Birth weight >=1250 g: no difference.

n_randomized: 1273 infants randomized; 1205 survived to primary outcome assessment
population: Preterm infants born before 29 weeks of gestation, randomized within 3 days after first enteral feeding; stratified by sex, gestational age (<27 weeks or 27 to <29 weeks), and center
intervention_dose_duration: Enteral emulsion providing DHA at 60 mg/kg body weight/day vs control soy emulsion without DHA; from randomization (within 3 days of first enteral feeding) until 36 weeks postmenstrual age
primary_outcome: Physiological bronchopulmonary dysplasia (oxygen-saturation monitoring in selected infants) at 36 weeks postmenstrual age or discharge home, whichever first
key_findings: Physiological BPD 291/592 (49.1%) DHA vs 269/613 (43.9%) control; adjusted RR 1.13 (1.02–1.25). 5-y FSIQ 95.4 vs 91.9 (adjusted difference 3.45, 0.38–6.53); no behaviour difference at 5 y.

lcpufa: DHA only (1.2 g/d algal oil to mother)
n_randomized: 461 mothers and 528 infants (232 mothers/273 infants to DHA; 229 mothers/255 infants to placebo)
population: Breastfed preterm infants born before 29 weeks' gestation (mean GA 26.6 weeks [SD 1.6]); mothers who were lactating and delivered before 29 weeks, enrolled within 72 hours of delivery; 16 Canadian NICUs
intervention_dose_duration: Maternal oral capsules providing 1.2 g/day DHA vs placebo capsules; from randomization to 36 weeks' postmenstrual age
primary_outcome: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia-free survival at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age
key_findings: Stopped early. BPD-free survival 54.9% vs 61.6% (RR 0.91, 0.80–1.04); BPD in survivors 41.7% vs 31.4% (RR 1.36, 1.07–1.73); mortality RR 0.61 (0.33–1.13). No Bayley-III difference at 18–22 mo.

n_randomized: 206 (101 AA:DHA, 105 control)
population: Infants born at less than 28 weeks' gestation (extremely preterm), enrolled at 3 university hospitals in Sweden (Dec 2016 to Dec 2019)
intervention_dose_duration: Enteral oil providing arachidonic acid (AA) 100 mg/kg/d and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) 50 mg/kg/d, started within 3 days after birth and continued until 40 weeks' postmenstrual age; control group received no supplementation (standard of care)
primary_outcome: Severe retinopathy of prematurity (stage 3 and/or type 1)
key_findings: Severe ROP 16/101 (15.8%) vs 35/105 (33.3%); adjusted RR 0.50 (0.28–0.91). BPD 48/101 vs 48/105. Larger white-matter volume at term (secondary).

population: GA <29 wk
intervention_dose_duration: ARA 100 + DHA 50 mg/kg/d from day 2 to 36 wk PMA
primary_outcome: Brain maturation (MRI)
key_findings: BPD 23/55 vs 30/55 (RR 0.77, 0.52–1.14); fewer days on respiratory support; ROP ≥3 3/55 vs 7/55; no Bayley-III difference at 2 y.

n_randomized: 110 preterm infants (55 per group)
population: Preterm infants with birth weight <1500 g but ≥1000 g, recruited in a neonatal intensive care unit (gestational age not reported in abstract)
intervention_dose_duration: Enteral DHA 75 mg/kg/day vs control high oleic sunflower oil, for 14 days via enteral feeding; double-blind parallel design
primary_outcome: Incidence of any stage of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP); secondary outcomes were severe ROP (stage ≥3) incidence and hospital stay
key_findings: No difference in any-stage ROP (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.49-1.27; P=0.33). Stage ≥3 ROP lower with DHA (RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.44-0.99; P=0.03); adjusted OR 0.10 (95% CI 0.011-0.886; P=0.04). Hospital stay similar between groups. Authors conclude enteral DHA may reduce stage 3 ROP.

n_randomized: 225 recruited; 214 randomized infants analysed intent-to-treat (DHA-group n = 105; control-group n = 109); 200 analysed per protocol
population: Preterm newborns with an expected functional gastrointestinal tract; recruited in two neonatal intensive care units of two tertiary hospitals. Gestational age and birth weight inclusion criteria not stated in abstract.
intervention_dose_duration: Enteral DHA 75 mg/kg body weight daily vs high-oleic sunflower oil (control), daily for 14 days starting from the first enteral feed after birth; randomized 1:1, double-blind, parallel-group
primary_outcome: Confirmed necrotizing enterocolitis (Bell's stage ≥ IIa). Abstract does not explicitly label a primary outcome; intent-to-treat treatment failure is also reported.
key_findings: Confirmed NEC lower in DHA-group vs control (0/100 vs 7/100; p = 0.007); RR = 0.93 (95% CI 0.881 to 0.981); risk difference -7% (95% CI -12.00 to -1.99); NNT = 15 (95% CI 8.3 to 50). ITT treatment failure lower in DHA-group (6/105 vs 16/109; p = 0.03; RR 0.905, 95% CI 0.826 to 0.991). Multivariate results remained significant. Adverse events (other than NEC) not different between groups.

n_randomized: 160 premature infants
population: Premature infants with gestational age <32 weeks and birth weight <1500 g who were at risk of ROP development (Tehran, Iran, 2013)
intervention_dose_duration: Intervention group: omega-3 300 mg daily; control group: sterile water as placebo. Start and duration not reported in abstract.
primary_outcome: Frequency and severity of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), defined by the International Classification of ROP. Abstract does not explicitly designate a primary outcome.
key_findings: ROP frequency 7.5% (omega-3) vs 20.0% (placebo), p = 0.021. Severity differed significantly (p = 0.001): omega-3 had grade I in 2 and grade II in 4; placebo had grade I in 6, II in 6, III in 4. Multivariate logistic regression (adjusted for gender, gestational age, birth weight): omega-3 associated with reduced ROP risk (p = 0.045).

n_randomized: 67 randomised (30 per group completed the study)
population: Preterm neonates with gestational age ≤32 weeks at birth and birth weight ≤1500 g, admitted to NICU
intervention_dose_duration: Enteral docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) supplementation vs control; dose, start timing and full duration not reported in abstract. IL-1β measured at baseline and after 10 days
primary_outcome: Not explicitly stated in abstract. Outcomes reported: NEC diagnosis and staging (modified Bell's criteria), percentage change in IL-1β levels, NICU length of stay, mortality
key_findings: Significant between-group difference in NEC diagnosis and staging (p=0.0001). IL-1β percentage change differed between groups (DHA 22 (73.3%) vs control 8 (26.7%), p=0.0001). NICU LOS lower in DHA group (21.63±6.67 vs 25.07±4.67 days, p=0.025). Mortality 3 (9.1%) DHA vs 4 (11.8%) control, p=1.0. Authors conclude enteral DHA may reduce NEC incidence via immunoregulation.

n_randomized: 71 randomized (76 initially enrolled)
population: Preterm neonates <34 weeks gestation and birth weight <1800 g, tertiary care hospital in Bangladesh, November 2022 to March 2024
intervention_dose_duration: Intervention: omega-3 LCPUFA capsule enterally, 40 mg/kg/day, added to enteral feeds within 48 h of first enteral feed, continued for 4 weeks. Control: no supplementation.
primary_outcome: Incidence of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)
key_findings: Overall ROP incidence similar: 37.1% intervention vs 41.6% control (p = 0.69). Severe ROP: 3 (23.1%) intervention vs 9 (60%) control (p = 0.049). Logistic regression (adjusted for ROP risk factors) showed no significant association between omega-3 LCPUFA and ROP incidence. Authors state supplementation does not reduce overall ROP but may lower severe ROP risk; study lacks power to confirm this.

n_randomized: 62 preterm infants (DHA n = 29; standard care n = 33)
population: Preterm infants < 34 weeks gestation (gestational age/birth weight inclusion details not stated in abstract)
intervention_dose_duration: Oral docosahexaenoic acid (omega-3 fatty acid) at 60 mg/kg daily (dose unit as printed in abstract: "60 mg/kg of."); start and duration not stated in abstract; control = standard care
primary_outcome: Incidence of NEC diagnosed by modified Bell's criteria
key_findings: Any NEC 14/29 vs 22/33; NEC ≥IIB 8/29 vs 19/33 (preprint Table 3); mortality 1/29 vs 5/33; neutropenia more frequent with DHA (6/29 vs 0/33).

n_randomized: 60 preterm infants randomized (DHA n = 31; placebo n = 29); term peers (n = 30) analysed for comparison only
population: Preterm infants, 24-34 weeks gestational age, supplementation beginning in the first week of life; term peers used as comparison group
intervention_dose_duration: Enteral DHA 50 mg/day in addition to standard nutrition vs placebo (standard neonatal nutrition); started in first week of life; continued to near discharge (blood sampled at baseline, full feedings, and near discharge)
primary_outcome: Not stated as a primary outcome in the abstract; blood fatty acid levels (DHA wt% and mol%) at baseline, full feedings and near discharge were analysed; feasibility, tolerability and efficacy were the study objectives
key_findings: Preterm infants had lower baseline DHA (p<0.0001). DHA group DHA rose from 3.33 to 4.09 wt% (2.88 to 3.55 mol%, p<0.0001); placebo unchanged (3.35 to 3.32 wt%; 2.91 to 2.87 mol%). At discharge preterm DHA remained below term peers (4.97 wt%; 4.31 mol%; p=0.0002). No differences in adverse events between groups. Authors conclude DHA supplementation is feasible and alleviates deficiency.

n_randomized: 30 randomised; 28 survivors completed dosing and sampling
population: Extremely-low-birth-weight (ELBW) infants; randomised within 72 h of age; median birth weight 806 g (of completers)
intervention_dose_duration: Once-daily buccal mucosa DHA+ARA drops: DHA 20 mg/kg/d + ARA 40 or 60 mg/kg/d (per arm as reported), or DHA 20 mg/kg/d + ARA 120 mg/kg/d, or placebo; 8 weeks duration
primary_outcome: Red blood cell phospholipid DHA (wt%) at 2 and 8 weeks of age (ARA was secondary)
key_findings: RBC DHA and ARA similar between groups at 2 wk (DHA 4.62 wt%, IQR 4.1-5.5, P=0.29; ARA 21.1 wt%, IQR 18.78-22.6, P=0.41) and 8 wk (DHA 6.0 wt%, IQR 5.1-7.1, P=0.57; ARA 20.1 wt%, IQR 18.3-23.1, P=0.63). DHA rose a median 31% from 2 to 8 wk (P<0.04); ARA did not change (P>0.6). Buccal DHA/ARA did not affect fatty acid levels.

n_randomized: 30 infants randomized to three groups (sunflower oil, n = 6 at 2 weeks; LCPUFA-120, n = 12; LCPUFA-360, n = 12 at 2 weeks). Total randomized number not stated in abstract.
population: Very low birth weight infants; median gestational age 28 weeks (IQR 27-30); median birth weight 1040 g (IQR 910-1245 g)
intervention_dose_duration: (1) LCPUFA-120: 40 mg/kg/day DHA + 80 mg/kg/day ARA (DHA:ARA 1:2); (2) LCPUFA-360: 120 mg/kg/day DHA + 240 mg/kg/day ARA; (3) sunflower oil placebo. Daily enteral dosing for 8 weeks or until discharge, whichever came first.
primary_outcome: Feasibility of providing a concentrated emulsified LCPUFA supplement; whole blood LCPUFA concentrations (wt%; g/100 g) at baseline, 2 weeks, and 8 weeks. Change in blood DHA and ARA from baseline were the reported outcomes of interest.
key_findings: At 2 weeks, change in blood DHA differed among groups (sunflower oil -0.63; LCPUFA-120 -0.14; LCPUFA-360 0.46 wt%; P = .002). Change in blood ARA also differed (P = .0002; LCPUFA-360 2.9 vs LCPUFA-120 0.1 vs sunflower oil -2.2). Changes from baseline to 8 weeks differed for DHA (P = .02) and ARA (P = .003). Authors conclude enteral LCPUFA supported higher blood DHA by 2 weeks and 360 mg combined DHA+ARA is likely necessary to reduce declines and allow increases over 8 weeks.

n_randomized: 31 randomised (40 mg/kg/day n=11; 80 mg/kg/day n=9; 120 mg/kg/day n=11); 23 non-randomised reference infants (no supplementation n=11; maternal DHA supplementation n=12)
population: Preterm infants born less than 30 weeks' gestational age
intervention_dose_duration: DHA as an emulsion at 40, 80 or 120 mg/kg/day via feeding tube, commenced within 4 days of first enteral feed; duration not stated in abstract
primary_outcome: Not stated in abstract (outcomes reported: tolerability (days of interrupted feeds, days to full enteral feeds), blood DHA and arachidonic acid (AA) levels, DHA level at study end)
key_findings: All DHA doses well tolerated, with no effect on days of interrupted feeds or days to full enteral feeds. Dietary DHA directly related to blood DHA, unrelated to AA. All randomised groups and maternal supplementation reference group prevented the end-of-study fall in DHA seen without supplementation.

n_randomized: 377 randomized and analysed (182 girls, 195 boys); 338 (89.7%) had complete primary outcome data. Of 2363 assessed, 982 eligible, 605 declined
population: Children born at <35 weeks' gestation, aged 10-16 months corrected age at enrolment; recruited from 9 NICUs at a large US pediatric academic center; median corrected age 15.7 months
intervention_dose_duration: Microencapsulated DHA 200 mg + arachidonic acid (AA) 200 mg daily vs microencapsulated corn oil placebo (one-to-one, fully masked); 6 months (trial conducted April 26, 2012 to March 24, 2017)
primary_outcome: Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, third edition (Bayley-III) cognitive composite score at 16-22 months corrected age
key_findings: No difference in Bayley-III cognitive score between DHA+AA and placebo (difference in change 0.5 [95% CI -1.8 to 2.8]; effect size 0.05; P = .66). Negative effect on language scores in children with lower birth weight (P = .03 for interaction) and on effortful control in households with income >$35,000 (difference -0.3 [95% CI -0.4 to -0.1]; P = .01). Motor and activity level unaffected.

n_randomized: 31 randomized; 28 of 31 had complete outcome data (analysed by intent to treat with mixed effects regression)
population: Toddlers aged 18-38 months born at ≤29 weeks' gestation, exhibiting ASD symptomology
intervention_dose_duration: Combined dietary DHA, EPA, and GLA (omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acid) supplementation vs placebo; 90-day duration. Dose not stated in abstract.
primary_outcome: Parent-reported sensory processing measured by the Infant/Toddler Sensory Profile (ITSP). The abstract does not explicitly designate a single primary outcome; analyses explored effects across ITSP sections and quadrants.
key_findings: Not statistically significant (p=0.13) but medium-to-large effect (effect size=0.57) for reduction in behaviors associated with sensory sensitivity; other ITSP scales had effect sizes 0.10 to 0.32. Authors state findings support larger randomized trials. Baseline: most atypical ITSP scores fell below the mean.
